title: Traversing, Searching, Updating, and Removing Collection Items
learningObjectives: Traverse collections systematically without skipping or repeating unintended items.
Search collections using a linear scan and recognize when keyed lookup is available.
Update an item while preserving the collection's intended structure.
Remove items safely while understanding how indexes can shift.
Choose a traversal or mutation approach that handles empty collections and boundary cases.

understand.concept: Traversal visits items in a defined sequence or order. Searching checks items against a target or condition. Updating changes a stored value. Removing changes collection membership or length and may shift indexes. These operations must follow the collection's rules and account for empty data, missing items, and mutation during iteration.
understand.whyItMatters: Collection operations are core to nearly every program: displaying records, finding a product, editing a profile, filtering a list, or deleting a completed task. Safe operation order prevents skipped items, invalid indexes, and unintended changes.
understand.analogy: Imagine checking every shelf in a storeroom, finding a labeled box, changing its label, or removing it. If you remove shelves/items while counting forward, the next item may slide into the position you just passed.
understand.analogyLimit: Collection APIs differ. Some structures support efficient removal by key or iterator; array-like structures may shift indexes; iteration rules vary by language. Always use the actual language's documented behavior.

explain.narrative: Traversal means visiting each element, often with a loop. A linear search compares each visited item with a target and can stop when it is found. Updating may be done by index, key, or reference, depending on the collection. Removing while traversing can change the remaining positions: if a forward loop increments after deleting the current element, the item shifted into that index may be skipped. Safer options include traversing backward for index-based removal, building a filtered collection, or using a collection's supported iterator/removal mechanism. For maps and sets, use their key/member operations rather than pretending they are indexed sequences. Empty and missing cases should be explicit.

examples.title: Traverse every item
examples.code:
const values = [4, 7, 9];
for (const value of values) console.log(value);
examples.explanation: The loop visits each element once in iteration order without manually changing an index.

examples.title: Linear search and early stop
examples.explanation: The search compares each value with the target and stops after a match. If no match occurs, found remains false.

examples.title: Update by index
examples.explanation: The second element is updated directly. The collection length and other values remain unchanged.

examples.title: Remove safely while iterating backward
examples.explanation: Moving backward means removing an item does not shift any unvisited earlier indexes.

examples.title: Search a map by key and update
examples.explanation: Map membership and update use the key. The check avoids updating a missing key accidentally.

commonMistakes: Incrementing a forward index after removing the current item and skipping the shifted item.
Assuming a search always finds the target.
Using an invalid index or missing key without checking the result.
Mutating a collection while iterating without understanding iterator rules.
Confusing changing an element with removing it from the collection.
Writing search code that fails to handle an empty collection.

guidedTask.title: Guided: Find, update, and remove matching values
guidedTask.instructions: Work through a list of scores and safely change its contents.
steps: Traverse the list and print each value.
Search for a target score; report found or not found.
Update one existing value by index.
Remove every value below a threshold using a safe strategy (backward loop or filtering).
Test the logic with an empty list and with no matches.
guidedTask.starterCode:
const scores = [12, 4, 18, 7, 3];
// Traverse, search, update, and safely remove values.

independentTask.title: Independent: Manage a small collection
independentTask.instructions: Create a program or pseudocode for a collection of tasks, names, inventory entries, or scores.
requirements: Search for one item and handle both match and no-match cases.
Update a found item without changing unrelated entries.
Remove one or more items using a safe mutation strategy.
Demonstrate empty collection and boundary/missing-item behavior.

hints: Use a simple loop when you need to inspect every item.
Search should have a clear result for both found and not found.
Check the target index/key before changing data.
When deleting from an indexed sequence, consider iterating backward or building a new filtered sequence.
A forward deletion loop may skip the item that shifts into the deleted index.
Test empty collections and targets that do not exist.

questions.prompt: What does traversal of a collection mean?
options: Visiting its items according to a defined iteration order
questions.answer: Visiting its items according to a defined iteration order
questions.explanation: Traversal systematically visits collection elements, commonly using a loop.

questions.prompt: What is a linear search doing?
options: Comparing visited items with a target or condition
questions.answer: Comparing visited items with a target or condition
questions.explanation: A linear search checks elements one by one until it finds a match or reaches the end.

questions.prompt: Why can removing an item during a forward index loop skip the next item?
options: Remaining items may shift left into the removed index
Removal always changes every item to null
questions.answer: Remaining items may shift left into the removed index
questions.explanation: If the loop increments after removal, it may move past the newly shifted item.

questions.prompt: Which strategy can safely remove matching values from an indexed sequence when index shifting is a concern?
options: Traverse indexes from the end toward the start
Always increment from index zero after each deletion
Remove the first value without checking it
questions.answer: Traverse indexes from the end toward the start
questions.explanation: Backward traversal keeps earlier, unvisited indexes stable when later items are removed.

questions.prompt: What should a search routine return or report if no target exists?
options: The last item regardless of match
questions.explanation: Search logic should explicitly represent failure to find a target rather than silently return an unrelated item.
